title: A Statistical Revamp Is About to Lower U.S. Inflation Readings at a Critical Moment
excerpt: The Bureau of Economic Analysis is changing how it calculates software, investment management, and legal services prices — a tweak that could reduce PCE inflation by two-tenths of a point just as the Fed weighs rate decisions.
body:
• The Bureau of Economic Analysis is changing how it calculates prices for software, investment management, and legal services in the PCE inflation index.
  • The changes are expected to reduce the Fed's preferred inflation measure by about two-tenths of a percentage point, according to former Fed economist Alan Detmeister.
  • Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has signaled he focuses on inflation "to the left of the decimal point," but even small changes could sway policy debates at the margin.
  • The revisions will take effect in September when the BEA annually updates the past five years of data.

The Methodology Shift

The Bureau of Economic Analysis is preparing to change how it measures prices in three categories within the Personal Consumption Expenditures index — the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge. The adjustments to software, investment management, and legal services calculations are set to take effect in September, when the agency annually revises five years of historical data.

The net effect, according to former Federal Reserve economist Alan Detmeister, will be to reduce PCE inflation by approximately two-tenths of a percentage point. In normal times, that would be a statistical footnote. In mid-2026, with core PCE above 3 percent and the Fed debating whether higher interest rates are necessary, even a small downward revision could tilt the policy debate.

What's Changing

On software, the BEA is adjusting how it accounts for computing power improvements — essentially giving more credit for quality gains in software products, which lowers the measured price increase. On investment management, the agency will use labor-market data rather than its previous methodology, which some economists note is subject to significant revisions. For legal services, the BEA will swap out Consumer Price Index data — which the Bureau of Labor Statistics has stopped publicly releasing due to collection challenges — for numbers from the Producer Price Index.

The software and investment changes will push inflation readings down. The legal services switch will push them up. On balance, the downward effects are expected to outweigh the upward ones.

Timing and Politics

The BEA has described the changes as routine adjustments to improve statistical accuracy. But the timing is charged. Inflation has run above the Fed's 2 percent target for more than five years — the longest such stretch since 1987-1994. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who took office in late May, has staked his credibility on restoring price stability.

"The goal is straightforward: to ensure the Fed is best positioned to achieve our objectives in this consequential time."

— Kevin Warsh, Federal Reserve Chairman

Warsh has said he prefers to focus on inflation "to the left of the decimal point," suggesting he won't be swayed by small methodology-driven changes. But within the Federal Open Market Committee, where officials are divided on whether to hold rates or hike, even a slight cooling in the headline number could provide cover for the dovish camp.

What Investors Should Watch

For Indian-American investors and NRIs with U.S. financial exposure, the inflation revision matters in concrete ways. Mortgage rates, currently at 6.55 percent, are directly tied to Fed rate expectations. A lower PCE reading could ease the path to rate cuts, improving borrowing conditions for homebuyers and reducing costs on variable-rate student loans.

The June PCE report, due July 30, will be the last before the September revisions take effect. Goldman Sachs and Pantheon Macro project core PCE to edge down to 3.3 percent from 3.4 percent — a step in the right direction, but still far from the 2 percent target. The question is whether the methodology changes accelerate the statistical journey back to normal, even as the underlying economic reality remains stubbornly inflationary.
